\[
\rho_s = \rho + A \sin\left(\frac{2\pi \rho}{\lambda} + \phi\right),
\quad \theta_s = \theta,
\qquad A = 4,\ \lambda = 24,\ \phi = 0^{\circ}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(\rho, \theta\): The polar coordinates around the image center, in pixels
- \(A, \lambda, \phi\): The amplitude, the wavelength and the phase

rho and theta are the polar coordinates of an output pixel around the image center, in pixels. It reads the source at the same angle, moved along the radius by a sine of its distance. Rings where the sine rises are stretched and rings where it falls are pressed, which looks like waves on water. This rule is PixelNexus's own. Each output pixel reads the source at the mapped position with bilinear interpolation, the inverse mapping of Gonzalez and Woods, so no holes appear.
